rule: order = the order of the code slides of the deck; the page tab lists the examples by name in this order; each runs as setup + listing, with the library defined in the page

library.import: import sen0401_ch10_lib_v1_1_0 as L, sen0401_ch10_p2p_v1_1_0 as P

setup.code:
# setup: the chapter library of the page (L = chapter 10 library, P = the wire code written independently of Bitcoin Core, R = the recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1); the page boots these names
import sen0401_ch10_lib_v1_1_0 as L
import sen0401_ch10_p2p_v1_1_0 as P
R = L.run()
src, seen = L.const, L.has

examples.name: The handshake: version first, verack to accept
examples.code:
# The recorded greeting between two test nodes running Bitcoin Core 31.1.
e = R['e1_handshake']
v = e['node_version']
# The messages arrive in a fixed order, version first.
seq = [c for t, c, n in e['sequence']]
# The version message names the software, the protocol and the chain height.
k = ('user_agent', 'version', 'start_height')
hello = tuple(v[x] for x in k)
print(hello)

examples.name: A message is a 24-byte header and a payload
examples.code:
# A verack message has no payload at all, so only the frame remains.
f = P.frame('verack', b'', 'main')
# Four fields make the frame: network magic, command, length and checksum.
n = int.from_bytes(f[16:20], 'little')
c = f[4:16].rstrip(b'\0').decode()
parts = (f[:4].hex(), c, n, f[20:].hex())
print(parts)

examples.name: Services: what a node offers
examples.code:
# Two nodes of the run, a full node and a pruned node, list their services.
full = R['networkinfo_A']['localservicesnames']
pruned = R['e10_pruned']['services']
# The pruned node has dropped the NETWORK flag: it keeps only recent blocks.
gone = [s for s in full if s not in pruned]
print(gone)

examples.name: DNS seeds hand out peer addresses
examples.code:
# The node asked eight DNS seeds for addresses and counted the IPv4 answers.
d = R['e11_dns_seeds']
n = [len(v['ipv4']) for v in d['answers'].values()]
# Each seed answered with twenty to thirty addresses; the default port is 8333.
f = 'core_src_kernel_chainparams.cpp'
port = src(f, 'nDefaultPort')
print((len(n), min(n), max(n), port))

examples.name: addr against addrv2
examples.code:
# Two peers asked for addresses, one with the old addr and one with addrv2.
a = R['e9_addr']
v2 = a['with_sendaddrv2']['addrv2']
# A reply never holds more than 23 percent of the address book.
np = 'core_src_net_processing.cpp'
cap = src(np, 'MAX_PCT_ADDR_TO_SEND')
# addrv2 adds a network id and variable length, so Tor and I2P fit.
print((v2['count'], v2['networks'], v2['addr_len'], cap))

examples.name: Connection types and their limits
examples.code:
# The node opened three kinds of links, each recorded with what it relays.
t = R['e8_types']
# Bitcoin Core keeps eight full-relay links and two block-relay-only links.
n = 'core_src_net.h'
full = src(n, 'MAX_OUTBOUND_FULL_RELAY_CONNECTIONS')
ro = src(n, 'MAX_BLOCK_RELAY_ONLY_CONNECTIONS')
# At most 125 links in all, counting those that call in.
total = src(n, 'DEFAULT_MAX_PEER_CONNECTIONS')
print((full, ro, total))

show.expected: [['addr-fetch', True, True, 'v2'], ['block-relay-only', False, False, 'v1'], ['outbound-full-relay', True, True, 'v2']]

examples.name: Headers first: 80 bytes a block
examples.code:
# A new node first asks a peer for headers, not for blocks.
h = R['e2_headers']
# One reply holds at most 2000 headers; the second reply held 101.
got = [h['first_count'], h['second_count']]
# A header has a fixed size, so the whole chain of headers is small.
print((got, h['header_size'], h['height']))

examples.name: Relay by wtxid and the fee filter
examples.code:
# The node announced two transactions, one cheap and one dear.
r = R['e5_relay']
k = r['invs']
lo, hi = r['feerate_low'], r['feerate_high']
rates = (round(lo, 1), round(hi, 1))
# A peer that sets a fee filter hears only of the dearer one.
ff = r['peer_feefilter_sat_per_kvb']
h = k['normal_wtxidrelay'], k['feefilter_5sat']
heard = (len(h[0]), len(h[1]))
print((ff, rates, heard))

examples.name: An orphan waits for its parent
examples.code:
# A child transaction is sent before its parent, so the node cannot take it.
o = R['e4_orphan']
early = o['child_in_mempool_after_child']
# The node asks the sender for the missing parent.
ask = hex(o['node_asked_for_parent'][0][0])
# Once the parent arrives, both sit in the memory pool.
k = 'parent_in_mempool_after', 'child_in_mempool_after'
late = tuple(o[x] for x in k)
print((early, ask, late))

examples.name: Every node has its own memory pool
examples.code:
# Node F holds six unconfirmed transactions; node G, never told, holds none.
m = R['e10_mempool_vs_utxo']
b = m['before_block']
pools = (b['F_mempool'], b['G_mempool'])
# Yet both agree on the set of unspent outputs.
same = m['utxo_hash_F'] == m['utxo_hash_G']
print((pools, same, m['utxo_count_F']))

examples.name: Compact blocks: 332 bytes instead of 3,062
examples.code:
# The test node sent one block of 13 transactions as a compact block.
c = R['e3_compact']
# Twelve short ids of 6 bytes stand for what the peer already holds.
ids = (c['short_id_count'], c['short_id_bytes'])
# Compare the bytes on the wire with the full block.
sizes = (c['cmpctblock_bytes'], c['full_block_bytes'])
ratio = round(sizes[0] / sizes[1], 4)
print(sizes)

examples.name: The block-finding race
examples.code:
# Blocks arrive on average every 600 seconds, at random moments.
delays = [1, 5, 10, 30, 60]
rival = L.rival_block_probability
# The chance that a rival block appears while yours still travels.
p = [round(rival(s), 4) for s in delays]
print(p)

examples.name: A parity part rebuilds a lost part
examples.code:
# Cut a message into four parts and add one parity part, their XOR.
parts = [b'compac', b't bloc', b'k mess', b'age!!!']
par = L.parity_code(parts)
# Lose any one part; the parity and the other three rebuild it.
lost = [parts[0], None, parts[2], parts[3]]
got = b''.join(L.rebuild(lost, par))
print(got)

show.expression: [i + 1 for i, x in enumerate(lost) if x is None]

examples.name: A light client checks a Merkle path
examples.code:
# A light client holds only headers; a full node sends one transaction with its path.
s = R['e6_spv']
e = R['e6_bloom_enabled']
# Three hashes lead from the transaction to the root in the header.
ok = s['root_from_path'] == s['header_root']
# The proof is far smaller than the block it comes from.
sizes = (s['proof_bytes'], e['full_block_bytes'])
print((s['path_len'], ok, sizes))

examples.name: Double-spend odds fall with each confirmation
examples.code:
# An attacker holds a share q of the hash rate and tries to catch up.
q = [0.1, 0.3]
zs = (0, 3, 6)
# Nakamoto's formula gives the chance of ever catching up from z blocks behind.
f = L.double_spend_probability
odds = [[round(f(x, z), 4) for z in zs] for x in q]
print(odds)

examples.code:
# A filter of 16 bits and 3 hash functions holds the patterns A and B.
r = L.toy_bloom_experiment()
# Everything added is found, but some strangers pass as well.

examples.name: Bloom filters are off by default
examples.code:
# Bitcoin Core 31.1 no longer offers Bloom filters unless asked.
d = R['e6_bloom_default']
has = 'BLOOM' in d['services_names']
# A peer that sends filterload anyway is disconnected.
gone = d['disconnected_after_filterload']
# With the option on, a 7-byte filter matched one transaction of five.
e = R['e6_bloom_enabled']
n = len(e['matched_txids'])
got = (e['filter_bytes'], n, e['block_txs'])
print((has, gone, got))

examples.name: Golomb coding sends differences
examples.code:
# Sort the numbers, send the first, then only the differences.
g = L.gcs_book_example()
# Differences need fewer bits than the numbers themselves: 8 instead of 10.
bits = (g['max_bits_original'], g['max_bits_deltas'])
print((g['deltas'], bits))

examples.name: Golomb-Rice coding is lossless
examples.code:
# Each difference is written as a unary quotient and p remainder bits.
v = [379, 476, 653, 849, 900]
r = L.rice_roundtrip(v, 7)
# Decoding returns the original list exactly, and the bits are fewer.
same = r['decoded'] == v
print((same, r['bits'], r['fixed_bits'], r['bytes']))

examples.name: A block filter rebuilt without Bitcoin Core
examples.code:
# The recorded filter of a regtest block, as Bitcoin Core built it.
f = R['e7_filter']
# The independent code rebuilds the same filter and the same filter header.
same = (f['my_filter_equal'], f['my_header_equal'])
# 104 elements fit in 275 bytes; all ten BIP 158 test vectors also pass.
k = ('n_elements', 'filter_bytes', 'bits_per_element')
per = tuple(f[x] for x in k)
print((same, per, L.bip158_vectors()))

examples.name: Transport v1 shows its magic, v2 hides it
examples.code:
# The same two nodes spoke the old transport once and the new one once.
t = R['e8_transport']
v1, v2 = t['v1'], t['v2']
# Can an eavesdropper see the network magic or the word version?
k = ('contains_magic', 'contains_version_command')
p1 = [v1[x] for x in k]
p2 = [v2[x] for x in k]
# The v2 stream looks like random bytes: near 8 bits of entropy per byte.
print((p1, p2, v2['entropy_first_4096']))

examples.name: Networks a node can reach
examples.code:
# A fresh node reaches the Internet over IPv4 and IPv6 only.
nets = R['networkinfo_A']['networks']
open_ = [x['name'] for x in nets if x['reachable']]
# A second node was set to use Tor: only the onion network is reachable.
o = R['e8_onion_node']['networks']
tor = [x[0] for x in o if x[1]]
print((open_, tor))
